source.title: Unlearning as multi-task optimization: A normalized gradient difference approach with an adaptive learning rate
source.authors: Zhi-Qi Bu; Xiaomeng Jin; Bhanukiran Vinzamuri; Anil Ramakrishna; Kai-Wei Chang; V. Cevher; Ming-Yi Hong

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates unlearning outcomes with benchmark metrics, including forgetting and retained utility, but does not apply post-unlearning recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for unlearning methods on target-set memorization and retained performance. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, or prompt changes. Statements about prior studies are not recorded as results here.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. It proposes NGDiff (normalized gradient difference with an automatic learning rate) and compares its forget/utility trade-off with GDiff (c=0.1/0.5/0.9), NPO and LossNorm. The comparison uses ROUGE-L-based Verbmem, Knowmem, Utility and TruthRatio on TOFU (forget10/retain90) and MUSE-NEWS, plus a CIFAR appendix. No recovery attack of any kind is applied: no relearning or fine-tuning, no activation edits, no quantization, no rephrasing, jailbreaks or in-context probes. So the results cannot show whether forgetting is deep or shallow. The paper treats low output-level ROUGE as successful unlearning. Its rows are its own method against baselines, so it assumes the claim rather than testing it. The reader's 'tests/T2' and its version A labels are rejected.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors frame unlearning as two-task multi-task optimization. They conclude that NGDiff, a normalized gradient difference with an automatic learning rate, improves forgetting while keeping utility relative to baselines on TOFU and MUSE-NEWS; they claim it 'consistently achieves the superior performance across all models'. In the Limitations they note that complete removal cannot always be guaranteed. Their own tables qualify the 'all models' claim: Falcon-1B TOFU utility of 0.428 is below their 70% threshold, and Table 6 MUSE-NEWS utility for Phi-1.5 and Falcon-1B is near zero as extracted.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes NGDiff, a normalized-gradient-difference unlearning method with an adaptive learning rate, and compares it with GDiff, NPO, and LossNorm. It does not test post-unlearning recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported results vary by model and dataset. The paper also reports sensitivity to fixed learning rates and improvements from its AutoLR scheduler.

fits_no_version.finding: On TOFU, NGDiff with AutoLR cuts Verbmem below 0.1 on all 5 models. It keeps utility at or above about 70% of No-unlearn on 4 of them; Falcon-1B utility is 0.428. In the recorded baseline columns, GDiff-0.5 and NPO often collapse utility: GDiff-0.5 is at 0.25-0.32 on four models and NPO at 0.000-0.136 on the three ~1B models. Some baselines fail to forget, e.g. GDiff-0.5 Verbmem 0.945 on Mistral-7B. The text adds that GDiff-0.9 and LossNorm fail to forget on Phi-1.5 and Mistral-7B. On MUSE-NEWS, NGDiff brings Knowmem below 70% of No-unlearn while keeping about 86% of utility on Llama2-7B and Mistral-7B. Appendix Table 6, as extracted, shows NGDiff's MUSE-NEWS utility at 0.001 (Phi-1.5) and 0.025 (Falcon-1B), against 0.372 and 0.386 without unlearning, even though the text says it 'still performs well'. The authors call baseline effectiveness highly model- and dataset-dependent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output-level (ROUGE) forget/utility trade-offs of gradient-based LLM unlearning methods depend strongly on model, dataset and learning rate. Normalizing the forget and retain gradients (NGDiff) with an automatic learning rate improves this trade-off in most tested settings. This is measured without any robustness or recovery attack.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: No post-unlearning recovery attacks are evaluated. Forgetting is measured with ROUGE-based output metrics rather than targeted-knowledge accuracy. No uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, omitted Table 1 results for GDiff-0.9, GDiff-0.1, LossNorm, and TruthRatio; Table 2 Verbmem results; Table 3 AutoLR ablation values; Table 6 results; and figure-only trajectories. The selected rows prioritize no-unlearn references, NGDiff, and GDiff-0.5/NPO comparisons on forgetting and utility.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover forgotten knowledge is untested. Targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance is not measured; only ROUGE-L recall on forget text and QA is reported. General ability is measured only on the retain split (and TruthRatio), not on a general benchmark.
No activation-direction ablation and no analysis of blocking versus deletion.
No quantization of the unlearned weights.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language or in-context probes.
NGDiff is not evaluated against any recovery attack, so it makes no robustness claim of the kind F describes.

record.verdict_notes:
Changes from the earlier verdict:
(1) The four grouped row_fixes items had list and range ids, which the merge refused. They are now 56 single-row items, R01-R56, one per row. Each item is set to versions ['none'] and state cannot_determine and gives the row's table value, checked against Tables 1-2. All 56 row values match the text.
(2) Every record row carried the undeclared version 'V1'. Each now has a row_fixes item mapping it to 'none', decided from what the row measures: output-level ROUGE forgetting or utility with no recovery attack, or a No-unlearn reference value.
(3) In fits_no_version I widened the row_ids to all own-method and baseline rows (R11-R40, R45-R56) and rewrote the finding so its numbers come from recorded rows. I also added the Table 6 caveat.
(4) In untested A I added that general ability is measured only on the retain split.
(5) authors_conclusion gains a note on where the tables qualify the 'all models' claim.

Kept unchanged: relation 'assumes', tranche T4, no labels, the untested list, and missing empty. Minor row metadata: the paper puts Phi-1.5 and GPT2-XL at about 1B (Sec. 5.3), where the record says 'not stated'. The 7B models were trained with LoRA rank 8 (App. F.3). In the extracted Table 6, the GDiff-0.5 and LossNorm columns for Phi-1.5 are identical, which may be an error in the paper or in extraction. The CIFAR appendix (Table 4) is not relevant. No original source is involved: this study is not listed in config.json originals. The study text contains no instructions to the reader.

versions.untested_parts: Post-unlearning attack resistance is not tested. The study reports ROUGE-based memorization and utility metrics, not targeted-knowledge accuracy.
No recovery fine-tuning or relearning set is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of access-blocking versus deletion is tested.
No quantization of unlearned weights is tested.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery is tested.
No resistance to the recovery attacks listed in the claim is tested.
